name: noodles (noodles-fasta FAI indexer)
workload: Build a samtools-compatible .fai index of the Homo sapiens GRCh38 primary assembly (Ensembl release 113, about 2.9 GiB uncompressed FASTA), warm page cache, 5 measured samples after 3 warmups, timed with zebrac v0.6.2; the noodles lane is a small CLI wrapper written by the z-fasta author around noodles-fasta 0.66.0 (fs::index then fai::fs::write).
claimed_speedup: Genome: 1.3640 s (noodles) vs 8.1614 s (samtools), about 6.0x faster (derived from page data); throughput 2203.5 MiB/s vs 368.3 MiB/s. Transcriptome (GENCODE v46, about 459 MiB): 0.4111 s vs 1.7112 s, about 4.2x (derived from page data). Proteome (UniProt UP000005640, about 13 MiB): 0.0176 s vs 0.0650 s, about 3.7x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: noodles wrapper: cargo build --locked --release with the default release profile (no LTO, no custom RUSTFLAGS), noodles-fasta 0.66.0, binary stripped. samtools 1.24 and HTSlib 1.24 built from source by tools/install.sh with plain ./configure and make (no explicit CFLAGS, so HTSlib's configure default applies, not an explicit -O3), binary stripped.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (named in the z-fasta README for the v0.3.5 run of 2026-10-10; the index REPORT.md itself names no CPU); Linux x86_64, warm cache.
stars_or_usage: 727 stars; noodles-fasta crate 484,738 downloads on crates.io
tradeoffs: Rust library family (FASTA, FASTQ, SAM/BAM/CRAM, VCF/BCF and more), not a drop-in samtools CLI; the .fai scanner is strict about uniform line widths (the z-fasta report shows noodles and samtools both exit non-zero on ragged, mixed-width or mixed CRLF FASTA).
caveats: The evidence lives in a competitor's repo: eneskemalergin/z-fasta is a Zig FASTA tool whose benchmark ranks itself first (0.3824 s on the genome, 3.6x faster than noodles); the noodles row is incidental. The lead named a REPORT.md Table 3 in z-fasta: it is bench/index/REPORT.md. The noodles lane is a custom wrapper, so its timing includes argument parsing and wrapper I/O, and the author states wrapper timings describe the wrapper CLIs rather than the upstream crates in isolation. samtools was not built with explicit -O3 and the HTSlib shared library is used, so the baseline is not a tuned -O3 build; same_opt_level is therefore null. Single machine, 5 samples, warm cache. No mechanism for noodles' lead over samtools is given in the report. Output byte-equality of the noodles .fai against samtools is not shown in the report text I read (the correctness table covers z-fasta against samtools). Peak RSS is equal (3.59 MiB noodles vs 9.31 MiB samtools on the genome).

name: sylph
workload: Multisample taxonomic profiling of shotgun metagenomes against large genome databases, CPU time and peak memory, as reported in the Nature Biotechnology paper (Shaw and Yu, 2025, 43(8):1348-59); a separate paper figure profiles against 85,205 prokaryotic plus 2,917,516 viral genomes.
claimed_speedup: Paper (search-result text of the PMC page): for multisample profiling sylph took more than 10-fold less CPU time than Kraken2 and used 30-fold less memory; sylph profiled against 85,205 prokaryotic and 2,917,516 viral genomes in under 1 minute with 16 GB RAM. README (repo page, not the paper): 'can be > 50x faster than other methods' (no baseline named) and about 5 GB RAM for GTDB-R232 (about 200k genomes).
compiler_and_flags: Rust; Cargo release profile sets panic=abort and lto=true. Kraken2 build flags and sylph build used in the paper are not visible to me.
tradeoffs: Abundance-corrected k-mer sketching: reports containment ANI and abundances against a pre-sketched database, species-level only, and trades per-read classification for sketch lookups. The README says it is about as precise and sensitive as marker-gene methods (MetaPhlAn, mOTUs) and has fewer false positives than Kraken, but no numbers are on the README.
caveats: Snippet only: the PMC, Nature and bioRxiv pages are unreachable from this environment (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the Kraken2 figures come from the text of a WebSearch result for the PMC page; paper tables, thread counts, CPU model, database sizes and the MetaPhlAn comparison were not seen. The two workloads differ in algorithm (sketch containment against genome database versus read k-mer classification), so the ratios compare tools with different outputs. The README names no baseline for its '>50x faster' claim. The sylph-test repo (bluenote-1577/sylph-test) lists scripts for paper Figs 1-4 and 6 and notebooks, and I identified no timing script there. The README says documentation moved to sylph-docs.github.io, which is blocked here. Mash, sourmash and MetaPhlAn timing rows were not confirmed.
found_via: seed-record pass: sylph README on github.com, then WebSearch text for the Nature Biotechnology paper 'Rapid species-level metagenome profiling and containment estimation with sylph' (PMC12339375), lead from the skani enricher
why_faster: k-mer sketching: subsampled k-mer sketches of reads and genomes (default compression c=200 in the changelog) with containment-based abundance estimation instead of classifying every read, multithreaded and multi-sample; per the paper abstract text and the repo README/CHANGELOG.

name: hunt (hunt-rs)
workload: File-name search over a home directory and the whole filesystem of one machine (about 2,762,223 files, including a network drive and an external drive): first match of a deeply nested hidden file, and all names containing 'SomeFile' from /.
claimed_speedup: First match under ~/: hunt --hidden --first --exact SomeFile ~/ 180.2 ms +/- 7.4 vs find ~/ -name SomeFile -print -quit 2.219 s +/- 0.071, 12.31 +/- 0.64 times faster. All matches from /: hunt -H SomeFile / 633.6 ms +/- 25.1 vs find / -name "*SomeFile*" 3.473 s +/- 0.144, 5.48 +/- 0.31 times faster. (fd, Rust sibling: 913.6 ms and 1.452 s.)
compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, strip, with rayon, crossbeam-channel, mimalloc and memchr (Cargo.toml, version 3.0.0); GNU find version and build flags not stated; the README does not say which hunt version produced the numbers.
tradeoffs: Simplified find: case-insensitive name match by default, results grouped and sorted, no regex or other find predicates, skips hidden directories unless --hidden, optional --ignore list; an opinionated tool rather than a find replacement.
caveats: README numbers only, measured with hyperfine on one unspecified machine (no CPU, kernel, filesystem, cache state, GNU find version or hunt version) over a tree that includes a network drive and an external drive. hunt is multithreaded while GNU find is single-threaded, and the tools do different work (hunt --first searches [current_dir, home_dir, root] in its own order, sorts and groups output, matches exact or substring names; find -name uses glob matching in depth-first order), so the first-match latency depends on where the file sits in each tool's traversal order. The benchmark script is benchmarks/run (for the 'run' task runner), not benchmarks.sh as the README says, and the lines I read compare hunt, a previous hunt 2.3.0 binary, fd and find (no locate). Last commit 2025-07-06 (about 15 months before the check). The locate row was omitted for the second case and quoted as 486.8 ms in the README text.
found_via: seed-record pass: lead from minifind enricher; README Benchmarks section of LyonSyonII/hunt-rs and benchmarks/run script
why_faster: Multithreaded parallel directory traversal (rayon work stealing, crossbeam channels) plus mimalloc and memchr substring search, per the README ('find did not perform any parallelism at all') and the Cargo.toml dependency comments.

name: walkdir and ignore walkers (dkorunic/bench_walk shootout)
baseline: GNU find (C), system find invoked as 'find <root>'
workload: Full recursive traversal of a shallow (--depth 1) clone of the mainline Linux kernel git tree, warm filesystem cache, Criterion (80 s warm-up, 400 s measurement per benchmark); single-threaded group and multi-threaded group.
claimed_speedup: Serial: walkdir 68.393 ms (best estimate) vs system find 90.621 ms, about 1.3x faster (derived from page data); walkdir_minimal 69.769 ms, ignore (serial unsorted) 73.457 ms, jwalk (serial) 77.011 ms, fts_walkdir 81.623 ms. Parallel winner: ignore (n threads, unsorted) 24.728 ms vs find 90.621 ms, about 3.7x faster (derived from page data); swdir 25.228 ms, jwalk 26.349 ms, about 2.7x faster than the best serial walker per the README.
compiler_and_flags: Cargo profiles release and bench: opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, strip symbols, panic abort (Cargo.toml); no target-cpu setting; GNU find version and build flags not stated; crates: walkdir 2.5, ignore 0.4.26, jwalk 0.8.1, swdir 0.11.3.
hardware: 8-core Xeon E5-1630 v3, 4-drive SATA RAID-10, ext4
stars_or_usage: 1 star; winners: walkdir (BurntSushi/walkdir, Unlicense/MIT, 680M crates.io downloads), ignore (crates/ignore in BurntSushi/ripgrep, Unlicense OR MIT, 189M downloads), swdir (nabbisen/swdir, Apache-2.0)
tradeoffs: Library crates, not CLIs: walkdir is the serial readdir/d_type walker, ignore adds gitignore handling and a work-stealing parallel walker, jwalk and swdir are other parallel walkers. The README notes the speedup of the parallel walkers is sublinear (2.7x on 8 cores) because traversal is syscall and I/O bound.
caveats: The lead calls these Go walkers; they are Rust crates (the repo benchmarks Rust walking crates and benchmarks system find as the only non-crate baseline). The find baseline is not like-for-like: src/lib.rs runs it as Command::new('find').arg(root).output(), so the find row includes process spawn and capturing all printed paths through a pipe, while the crate rows only iterate entries (for _ in WalkDir::new(root) {}) without printing; the README itself says find 'additionally pays process-spawn and output-formatting overhead'. That asymmetry alone could account for the 1.3x serial gap, so the serial win over find is weak; the 3.7x parallel win is mostly threads against a single-threaded find. GNU find version, flags and glibc are unstated. Single machine and one tree. I report ignore as the headline winner against find; walkdir is the best serial walker. The ignore entry may overlap with ripgrep's existing record.
found_via: seed-record pass: repo README results table and src/lib.rs find_walkdir of dkorunic/bench_walk (lead from the walker shootout)
why_faster: Per the README: walkdir, ignore and jwalk read each directory once and use the d_type field from readdir(3), so they recurse without extra stat calls; ignore, swdir and jwalk additionally traverse in parallel with work stealing on 8 cores.

name: ferromark
baseline: md4c (C); cmark (C) in a second report
workload: UTF-8 Markdown to complete HTML on a frozen 57-document corpus (37 to 113,609 bytes, CommonMark and shared GFM subset: tables, strikethrough, task lists), geometric mean of per-document time ratios, fresh and reuse lifecycles, parse plus render plus output destruction timed.
claimed_speedup: Native Linux x86-64 report 2026-09-24 (AMD EPYC 7763): md4c reaches 0.31x (fresh) and 0.29x (reuse) of Ferromark v2 throughput on the 50 documents with matching output, so Ferromark is about 3.2x and 3.4x faster (derived from page data); on the 14 documents where all six engines agree md4c is 0.24x fresh and 0.20x reuse (about 4.2x and 5.0x, derived from page data). Held-out half of the corpus (24 documents), default builds: 3.05x fresh, 3.22x reuse. Second report, blacksmith Linux x86-64 (2026-10-01, all 57 documents, AMD EPYC): vs md4c 2.95x fresh and 3.06x reuse, vs cmark 5.70x and 6.25x, vs cmark-gfm 6.15x and 6.67x (Comrak, a Rust sibling, 5.10x).
compiler_and_flags: Native harness: all Rust crates built with one pinned nightly toolchain, -C target-cpu=generic (x86-64 baseline; Ferromark, memchr and Highway still pick SSSE3/AVX2 paths at run time), release optimization, fat LTO, codegen-units=1, panic=abort; md4c and C/C++ support compiled with clang -O3 (Ubuntu clang 18.1.3), no PGO and no cross-language LTO in the default build; all engines share mimalloc and md4c's allocations are redirected to it. Manual comparison (blacksmith report, prepare-native.py): cmark library built by CMake Release with -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS_RELEASE=-O3 (GNU 13.3.0 at /usr/bin/cc), its worker adapter compiled with clang -O3, system malloc; Rust worker built with cargo build --release --locked and RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=generic'.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor, 4 vCPUs (GitHub-hosted runner, Linux 6.17.0-1022-azure) for the native harness; the blacksmith manual-comparison report names only 'AMD EPYC, 15.4 GB RAM, Linux 6.6.141' (4 vCPU runner).
tradeoffs: Markdown to HTML/JSX with secure defaults, CommonMark and GFM plus opt-in Ferromark Flavored Markdown; the benchmark disables optional syntax and renderer extras (heading IDs, callouts) to measure engine throughput, which is not the secure product default. Extra syntax adds parsing work.
caveats: First-party harness by the project author, with a very new, small project (9 stars) and many internal rewrites (963 commits, v1 and v2 controls). Engine outputs differ: only 14 of 57 documents agree across all six engines and 50 agree across the five with matching renderer options, so the 'all 57' ratios compare different outputs; the report says a throughput result does not establish conformance, and the manual-comparison table marks md4c with an asterisk for differing output. Rust is built for generic x86-64 while md4c is not PGO-built and not LTO'd; the shared-mimalloc control is not a stock system-malloc comparison, and in the manual comparison cmark runs with system malloc. Ferromark's own PGO build is shipped, md4c's is not, and PGO rows are only comparable with PGO rows. Timing is a short balanced profile (3 process rounds) in the second report, whose authors say it has less timing evidence than their standard profile. Runs on shared cloud runners. The README's '57-document comparison leads every measured library' claim page (ferromark.dev/guide/benchmarks) is blocked here; numbers come from the checked-in reports. Only the CPU model of the 2026-09-24 report is fully named.
found_via: seed-record pass: ferromark README 'native-benchmarks' section, then docs/reports/2026-09-24-native-linux-x86-64/README.md and docs/reports/2026-10-01-blacksmith-linux-x86-64/README.md in sebastian-software/ferromark
why_faster: README: arena allocation, reusable buffers, specialized byte scans, and SIMD reduce parser and renderer work; the harness also measures a reuse lifecycle (arena reset, borrowed output) separately from fresh calls.

name: base64-simd (Nugine/simd)
baseline: GNU coreutils base64 (/usr/bin/base64, C), via the uutils coreutils base64 command that adopted base64-simd
workload: Encode a single-line 4 GB file (/tmp/oneline_4G.txt) with the uutils coreutils base64 applet built on base64-simd versus /usr/bin/base64 and the previous uutils build, hyperfine -N --warmup 3, 10 runs.
claimed_speedup: uutils coreutils base64 with base64-simd 3.146 s +/- 0.037 vs /usr/bin/base64 4.901 s +/- 0.054, 1.56 +/- 0.02 times faster; vs the previous uutils build 5.998 s +/- 0.055, 1.91 +/- 0.03 times faster; user CPU 1.208 s vs 3.904 s for GNU (derived from page data: about 3.2x less user time), system time 1.937 s vs 0.996 s.
compiler_and_flags: uutils built with ./target/release/coreutils (cargo release profile of the coreutils workspace); GNU base64 version and build flags not stated.
stars_or_usage: 268 stars; base64-simd crate 164,897,007 downloads on crates.io; used by uutils coreutils (uucore features 'encoding' and 'checksum')
tradeoffs: Part of the Nugine/simd monorepo (base64-simd, hex-simd, base32-simd, unicode-simd, uuid-simd, vsimd); SIMD paths are chosen at compile time or by runtime detection ('detect' feature) with a fast fallback. The latest crates.io release (0.8.0) dates from 2022-12-28 while the repo was committed to as late as 2026-08-30.
caveats: No comparison against aklomp/base64, Turbo-Base64 or fastbase64 was found. The project's own harness (Nugine/simd-benches, benches/base64.rs and Cargo.toml) compares base64-simd only against Rust crates (radix64, base64, base64ct, data-encoding, based64), and its published results live on a github.io page that is blocked here. The only C-baseline number is a maintainer's PR comment (uutils/coreutils #8578, 2025-09-08) with no machine description and no GNU version; the end-to-end CLI time also includes the uutils I/O path (system time is higher than GNU's), so 1.56x understates the encoder gap, while the 1.91x gain over the previous uutils build is a before/after on the same program. GNU base64 is not in the listed baselines (aklomp/base64, Turbo-Base64, fastbase64).
found_via: seed-record pass: lead from the uutils coreutils base64 win; uutils/coreutils PR #8578 'base64: improve perfs by using the base64-simd crate', Nugine/simd README and Nugine/simd-benches sources
why_faster: SIMD-accelerated encode/decode: the README says the crates select SIMD functions automatically when available and cites Wojciech Mula's 0x80.pl base64 articles as the algorithm source; GNU base64 uses a scalar gnulib routine (my inference, not stated on the page).
